# Data wrangling {#sec-m1-manipulacao} From here on we use the course's real dataset: the **TKU of coastal shipping** (ANTAQ, 2025), with 732 records of pairs of port facilities. TKU (*tonelada-quilômetro útil*) is the cargo tonnage times the distance carried, in tonne-km. The file is listed in [Example data](a-dados.qmd) and is in the repository, in `dados/`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(readxl) library(stringr) ``` ::: ## Reading ### Spreadsheets ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bruto <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx") dim(bruto) #> [1] 732 12 names(bruto) #> [1] "Ano" "Perfil da Carga" #> [3] "Grupo de Mercadoria (SH2)" "País de Origem" #> [5] "UF de Origem" "Cidade de Origem" #> [7] "Instalação de Origem" "País de Destino" #> [9] "UF de Destino" "Cidade de Destino" #> [11] "Instalação de Destino" "TKU\n(t x km)" ``` ::: Look at the name of the last column: `TKU\n(t x km)`, with a line break and brackets. Names like this force you to write `` `TKU\n(t x km)` `` with backticks in every reference. The first thing to do with any spreadsheet is to standardise the names: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bruto |> janitor::clean_names() |> names() #> [1] "ano" "perfil_da_carga" #> [3] "grupo_de_mercadoria_sh2" "pais_de_origem" #> [5] "uf_de_origem" "cidade_de_origem" #> [7] "instalacao_de_origem" "pais_de_destino" #> [9] "uf_de_destino" "cidade_de_destino" #> [11] "instalacao_de_destino" "tku_t_x_km" ``` ::: `janitor::clean_names()` turns everything into lower case, replaces spaces and punctuation with `_` and removes accents. The names become usable, but are still long. Since we know the structure of the file, we will set short names **by position**, guarded by a check. If ANTAQ changes the number of columns in the next release, the script stops instead of renaming wrongly. The new names are year, cargo profile, HS2 commodity group, then country, state, city and facility of origin and of destination, and the TKU: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2", "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem", "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino", "tku") base <- bruto stopifnot(ncol(base) == length(colunas)) names(base) <- colunas dplyr::glimpse(base) #> Rows: 732 #> Columns: 12 #> $ ano 2025, 2025, 2025, 2025, 2025, 2025, 2025, 2025, 202… #> $ perfil "Carga Conteinerizada", "Carga Conteinerizada", "Ca… #> $ sh2 "CT-Contêineres", "CT-Contêineres", "CT-Contêineres… #> $ pais_origem "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "… #> $ uf_origem "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM", "AM… #> $ cidade_origem "Itacoatiara", "Itacoatiara", "Manaus", "Manaus", "… #> $ instalacao_origem "IP4 Itacoatiara", "Terminais Fluviais do Brasil", … #> $ pais_destino "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "Brasil", "… #> $ uf_destino "PR", "CE", "SP", "BA", "RJ", "PE", "CE", "PR", "SC… #> $ cidade_destino "Paranaguá", "São Gonçalo do Amarante", "Guarujá", … #> $ instalacao_destino "Paranaguá", "Terminal Portuário do Pecém", "Santos… #> $ tku 4213386.6, 725465.9, 8332538649.4, 1600854068.7, 15… ``` ::: Still at this stage, a filter worth explaining: **132 of the 732 records have TKU equal to zero**. They are combinations of commodity and cargo profile with no flow in the period, published as empty rows with `-` in the identification fields. They are analysed in detail in @sec-m1-limpeza; here we just set them aside. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::count(tem_fluxo = tku > 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} base <- base |> dplyr::filter(tku > 0) nrow(base) #> [1] 600 ``` ::: If you prefer to rename by the original name, explicitly: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base <- bruto |> dplyr::rename( ano = Ano, perfil = `Perfil da Carga`, sh2 = `Grupo de Mercadoria (SH2)`, uf_origem = `UF de Origem`, cidade_origem = `Cidade de Origem`, tku = `TKU\n(t x km)` ) ``` ::: Other useful arguments of `read_excel()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} readxl::read_excel("arquivo.xlsx", sheet = "Dados") # sheet by name readxl::read_excel("arquivo.xlsx", skip = 3) # skips decorative header rows readxl::read_excel("arquivo.xlsx", n_max = 1000) # only the first rows (for inspection) readxl::read_excel("arquivo.xlsx", col_types = "text") # reads everything as text (avoids coercion) readxl::read_excel("arquivo.xlsx", na = c("", "-", "n/d")) # what should become NA ``` ::: ### Text files ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} csv <- readr::read_csv("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) dim(csv) #> [1] 732 12 names(csv) |> head(4) #> [1] "Ano" "Perfil da Carga" #> [3] "Grupo de Mercadoria (SH2)" "País de Origem" ``` ::: For files in the Brazilian format, with `;` as separator and a decimal comma, use `read_csv2()`. Give the *encoding* when the file comes from a legacy system: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} readr::read_csv2("arquivo.csv", locale = readr::locale(encoding = "latin1")) ``` ::: ### Large files: `duckplyr` `readr` and `read_excel` load everything into memory. When the file has millions of rows (GTFS, GPS data, toll records, routing matrices), it is worth using `duckplyr`, which runs the query in **DuckDB** and brings only the result into memory. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(duckplyr) # reading is "lazy": nothing is loaded yet grande <- duckplyr::read_csv_duckdb("dados/roteamento_milhoes.csv") resultado <- grande |> dplyr::filter(uf_destino == "PR") |> dplyr::summarise(tku = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE), .by = uf_origem) |> dplyr::collect() # only here is the query run ``` ::: The syntax is the same as `dplyr`; the difference is `collect()` at the end, which materialises the result. In module 3 we compare the processing time of the two approaches with `system.time()` on a routing dataset. ::: {.callout-note} ## Which package to use | Situation | Tool | |:--|:--| | Up to ~1 million rows, code other people will read | `dplyr` | | Files that do not fit in memory, queries with filters and aggregation | `duckplyr` / `duckdb` | | Intensive wrangling with many operations per group | `data.table` | The three live together in the same script: it is common to read with `duckplyr`, aggregate, `collect()` and carry on in `dplyr`. ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## About `data.table` `data.table` is generally **faster** than `dplyr` for heavy wrangling (many `group_by`s, tables with tens of millions of rows). The reason it is not this course's main package is teaching, not technical: its syntax (`DT[i, j, by]`, with unquoted column references and operators such as `:=`) is more compact but less readable for people who are learning. If after the course you decide to move a whole script to `data.table` for performance, any AI assistant (@sec-m1-ambiente) reliably converts a `dplyr` snippet to `data.table`, because it is a mechanical translation between equivalent syntaxes. Check the result against the same anchor totals as in the previous chapter. ::: ## The `dplyr` verbs ### `select()`: choose columns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::select(uf_origem, uf_destino, tku) |> head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dplyr::select(base, tidyr::starts_with("uf")) # by prefix dplyr::select(base, tidyr::contains("cidade")) # by part of the name dplyr::select(base, -pais_origem, -pais_destino) # remove dplyr::select(base, carga = perfil) # select and rename dplyr::select(base, dplyr::where(is.numeric)) # by type ``` ::: ### `filter()`: choose rows ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::filter(uf_destino == "PR") |> nrow() #> [1] 32 base |> dplyr::filter(uf_origem == "AM", tku > 1e9) |> # the comma means "and" dplyr::select(cidade_origem, uf_destino, tku) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::filter(uf_destino %in% c("PR", "SC", "RS")) |> # South region nrow() #> [1] 130 base |> dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(perfil, "Granel")) |> dplyr::count(perfil) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::filter(uf_origem != uf_destino) |> # excludes flows within a state nrow() #> [1] 558 ``` ::: ### `mutate()`: create and change columns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base <- base |> dplyr::mutate( tku_bi = tku / 1e9, ligacao = stringr::str_c(uf_origem, " > ", uf_destino), interestadual = uf_origem != uf_destino, faixa = dplyr::case_when( tku >= 1e9 ~ "alto", tku >= 1e6 ~ "médio", .default = "baixo" ) ) base |> dplyr::select(ligacao, tku_bi, faixa) |> head(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ### `arrange()`: sort ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku)) |> dplyr::select(ligacao, cidade_origem, cidade_destino, tku_bi) |> head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ### `summarise()` and grouping ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::summarise( ligacoes = dplyr::n(), tku_total = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE), tku_medio = mean(tku, na.rm = TRUE), tku_max = max(tku, na.rm = TRUE) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Grouping is the most used operation of all. The modern syntax uses the `.by` argument: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} por_uf_destino <- base |> dplyr::summarise( ligacoes = dplyr::n(), tku_bi = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e9, .by = uf_destino ) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi)) por_uf_destino |> head(10) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: The equivalent with `group_by()`, which you will see in older material: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::group_by(uf_destino) |> dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e9) |> dplyr::ungroup() ``` ::: Grouping by more than one variable, with a percentage share: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::summarise(tku = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(perfil, uf_destino)) |> dplyr::mutate(part = tku / sum(tku), .by = perfil) |> dplyr::filter(part > 0.10) |> dplyr::arrange(perfil, dplyr::desc(part)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Note that `mutate(..., .by = ...)` computes **within the group without collapsing the table**. It works like a calculated field in a pivot table. ### `count()`, `distinct()`, `slice_max()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::count(perfil, sort = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::distinct(uf_origem) |> nrow() #> [1] 18 base |> dplyr::slice_max(tku, n = 3) |> dplyr::select(ligacao, tku_bi) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} base |> dplyr::slice_max(tku, n = 1, by = uf_destino) |> dplyr::select(uf_destino, ligacao, tku_bi) |> head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Reshaping: *long* ↔ *wide* Tables for human reading are **wide** (one column per category); tables for analysis and charts are **long** (one row per observation). `tidyr` converts between the two forms. ### *Long to wide*: the OD matrix ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} od_longo <- base |> dplyr::filter(uf_origem != uf_destino) |> dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e9, .by = c(uf_origem, uf_destino)) head(od_longo, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} od_largo <- od_longo |> tidyr::pivot_wider( names_from = uf_destino, values_from = tku_bi, values_fill = 0 ) |> dplyr::arrange(uf_origem) od_largo ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: This is exactly the structure of an **origin–destination matrix**, ready to export to Excel or convert into a `matrix`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- as.matrix(od_largo[, -1]) rownames(m) <- od_largo$uf_origem round(m[1:5, 1:5], 2) #> PR CE SP BA RJ #> AL 0.00 0.04 0.43 0.06 2.41 #> AM 0.56 1.03 12.40 1.60 2.37 #> BA 0.34 0.34 2.51 0.00 0.40 #> CE 0.07 0.00 3.70 0.27 0.77 #> ES 0.07 3.91 0.76 0.02 0.68 ``` ::: ### *Wide to long*: back to the analytical form ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} od_largo |> tidyr::pivot_longer( cols = -uf_origem, names_to = "uf_destino", values_to = "tku_bi" ) |> dplyr::filter(tku_bi > 0) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi)) |> head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: A frequent case with SIDRA and Census data: several year columns that should be a single `ano` (year) column. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pop <- data.frame( municipio = c("Paranaguá", "Santos"), pop_2010 = c(140469, 419400), pop_2022 = c(156174, 418375) ) pop |> tidyr::pivot_longer( cols = tidyr::starts_with("pop_"), names_to = "ano", names_prefix = "pop_", names_transform = list(ano = as.integer), values_to = "populacao" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Exporting results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dir.create("resultados", showWarnings = FALSE) # CSV in the international standard (decimal point) readr::write_csv(por_uf_destino, "resultados/tku_por_uf_destino.csv") # CSV to open in Excel set to Portuguese (semicolon, decimal comma) readr::write_csv2(por_uf_destino, "resultados/tku_por_uf_destino_excel.csv") # Excel, with one sheet per table writexl::write_xlsx( list( "TKU por UF" = por_uf_destino, "Matriz OD" = od_largo ), "resultados/cabotagem_2025.xlsx" ) # R's native format: keeps types exactly saveRDS(base, "resultados/cabotagem_limpa.rds") base2 <- readRDS("resultados/cabotagem_limpa.rds") # Open and efficient format, to exchange with Python/QGIS arrow::write_parquet(base, "resultados/cabotagem.parquet") ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Which format to deliver - **Excel (`.xlsx`)**: when the recipient will open and read it. Use named sheets. - **CSV**: when the file feeds another system. Agree on the separator first. - **RDS**: between steps of your own workflow. Fast and with no loss of types. - **Parquet**: large datasets shared between tools. - In the following modules come `.gpkg` and `.shp`, for spatial data. :::
